lab_title: AR Lab: Apparent Retrograde Motion of Mars (and Comparison to Jupiter & Saturn)
top_level_objectives: Explain why Mars appears to move westward during retrograde loops when viewed from Earth.
Connect retrograde motion to relative orbital speeds in a heliocentric model.
Contrast the size of retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn using their different orbital radii.
Interpret observational sky-traces (constellation-by-constellation drift) using an intuitive Earth–Mars geometry model.

scenes.scene_name: Night-Sky Observation Setup: Mars’s Eastward Drift
scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the baseline expectation: outer planets appear to drift slowly eastward relative to background stars.
key_visuals: AR night sky with labeled constellations
Mars marker with a slowly advancing path line across the star field
Timeline control indicating several consecutive nights (accelerated)
student_actions: Identify the background constellation anchors near Mars.
Track Mars’s position over the displayed nights and describe the direction of motion relative to the stars.
Predict what should happen next if the pattern stays the same.

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students witness the puzzle moment when Mars slows, stops, and reverses into westward motion.
key_visuals: Mars path line that thickens as motion slows
Motion arrows that change from eastward to westward
Overlay text: “Apparent retrograde” and a marker at the turnaround point
student_actions: Observe the interval where Mars’s eastward motion decreases to zero.
Record (in words) what changes at the reversal point.
Explain in plain language what “retrograde” means observationally (from Earth).

scenes.scene_name: Retrograde Loop Comprehension: Putting Mars Back in Context
scenes.brief_purpose: Help students interpret the full loop as a sky-trace that returns toward earlier positions rather than a one-time reversal.
key_visuals: Complete loop path drawn across multiple nights
Ghosted positions of Mars at key dates (before, during, after)
Optional simple comparison: “Against the stars” vs “In real space” (as a conceptual label)
student_actions: Describe the overall shape of the apparent motion (loop) and how long it persists.
Match key dates to points on the loop (start, middle, end).
State a hypothesis: what Earth-relative cause might produce a loop.

scenes.brief_purpose: Transition to a heliocentric perspective where the loop emerges naturally from relative motion.
key_visuals: Camera moves to a solar-system overview
Sun at center with Earth and Mars on circular/elliptical orbit tracks
Earth moving faster on an inner orbit; Mars slower on an outer orbit
Projected “line of sight” showing how Earth’s changing viewpoint creates the apparent sky path
student_actions: Identify which planet is on the faster (inner) orbit and which is slower (outer).
Describe the moment Earth overtakes Mars geometrically.
Connect this overtaking to why Mars appears to reverse direction from Earth.

scenes.brief_purpose: Solidify the causal idea using an accessible analogy (cars) that maps directly to angular apparent motion.
key_visuals: AR overlay showing two moving-lane car icons labeled Earth (inner lane) and Mars (outer lane)
Arrow directions illustrating faster overtaking and apparent backward drift
Bridge text: “Different real motion vs shared viewing motion”
student_actions: Match the analogy to the astronomical case: which car corresponds to which planet.
Explain why the observer’s own motion changes the perceived direction even if the other object keeps moving forward.
Use one sentence to restate the retrograde cause in relative-motion terms.

scenes.scene_name: Compare with Jupiter and Saturn: Smaller Retrograde Loops
scenes.brief_purpose: Use the outside view to compare how retrograde magnitude depends on relative orbital speed differences.
key_visuals: Same solar-system overview with Jupiter and Saturn added (scaled appropriately)
Smaller loop overlays on the sky-trace for Jupiter and Saturn compared to Mars
student_actions: Observe that Jupiter/Saturn loops are less dramatic and note when compared to Mars.
Reason: infer how farther distance reduces the relative-motion effect.
State why retrograde still occurs but with smaller apparent direction changes for outer planets farther out.
